newsitem.title: UK: British opposition retreats over new royal yacht.
newsitem.headline: British opposition retreats over new royal yacht.

text.p: Britain's oppostion Labour Party, striving to avoid offending pro-monarchy voters in an election year, retreated on Sunday from a pledge not to spend tax money on a new royal yacht.
But a senior Labour spokesman on economics said the decision on the 60 million pound ($100 million) project would have to be weighed against competing claims for new schools and hospitals.

In what political analysts saw as a vote-catching move, the Conservative government announced on Wednesday that it would order a new luxury craft in which the Queen could make state visits to replace the 44-year-old Britannia, now on its way to the Gulf and Hong Kong on its final voyage.

Labour, way out in front in public opinion polls ahead of a general election that must be held no later than May 22, has been trying to shed its image as a tax-and-spend party by pledging to keep a tight rein on public spending if it wins.
On Saturday, Labour defence spokesman John Reid told BBC television the party would have more important priorities.

"We will not fund out of public expenditure 60 million pounds for a royal yacht when there are demands such as hospitals, the health service and education which a Labour government will be expected to meet," he said.

But hours later, economics spokesman Alistair Darling said in another BBC interview that the decision to refuse funds for the project had not been taken. "The royal yacht could be an asset for the country," he said.
"But to rule out any contribution from the private sector or other ways of funding it at this stage, over a year before the contract would have to be signed, seems to us to be rather shortsighted."
"This project, the royal yacht, has to be judged alongside others such as schools and hospitals, for example," he added.
Labour's ambivalence on the issue drew instant reaction from its political opponents.
Finance minister Kenneth Clarke said: "There appears to be the clear line yesterday they weren't going to pay for it, and there seemed to be an extremely unclear line from Alistair rowing back."

The Mail on Sunday newspaper quoted unnamed royal aides as saying Queen Elizabeth was unhappy about the way that Defence Secretary Michael Portillo made the announcement about the yacht last week because it dragged the royal family into the pre-election battle.
But Portillo said: "We believe we should be supporting the Monarchy and Britain and Britain's image in this way."
The Conservatives say they want a replacement for the Britannia in time for Queen Elizabeth's Golden Jubilee in 2002.

Lord Ashbourne, Conservative chairman of the all-party Royal Yacht Parliamentary Group, said if Labour did refuse public money, the project might still be on. "It's not the end of the world. If a Labour government won't cough up the money, it's possible for the yacht to be funded by private money," he said.
The 6,000-tonne Britannia, with 234 crew, is on its way to Hong Kong to mark the handover of the territory to China on July 1. The yacht will be decomissioned later in the year.
Britannia costs 10 million pounds ($16 million) a year to run, but supporters say entertaining on it has helped secure two billion pounds ($3.2 billion) in exports over the past decade.
